汉.note:
Eastern Han (25–220), capital Luoyang. In the Yongyuan era under Emperor He, Dou Xian crushed the Northern Xiongnu and Ban Chao brought the Western Regions to submission, and the empire reached its greatest extent.
In the middle and later periods power passed back and forth between consort families and eunuchs; there were two Partisan Prohibitions, in 166 and 169. In 184 the Yellow Turbans rose, and in 188 the provincial Inspectors were turned into Governors, letting regional power grow.
In 189 Emperor Ling died; He Jin, plotting to destroy the eunuchs, was killed, and Dong Zhuo entered the capital, deposed one emperor and set up Emperor Xian. From then on the emperor was held in turn by Dong Zhuo and Li Jue until Cao Cao brought him to Xu in 196.
The warlords still nominally followed the Han calendar until Emperor Xian abdicated in favour of Cao Pi in 220 and the Han came to an end.

黄巾.note:
Zhang Jue of Julu spent more than ten years preaching the Way of Great Peace, gathering several hundred thousand believers organised in thirty-six divisions. In the 2nd month of 184 they rose on the same day under the slogan "The Blue Heaven is dead, the Yellow Heaven shall rise; in the year jiazi the world will have great fortune", and twenty-eight commanderies in seven provinces responded.
The court sent Huangfu Song, Zhu Jun and Lu Zhi against them: the forces in Yingchuan, Runan, Nanyang and Dong Commandery were crushed one after another, and in winter Zhang Liang and Zhang Bao were defeated and killed at Guangzong and Xiaquyang, ending the main rising. Remnants (the Qing Province, Black Mountain, Baibo and Runan Yellow Turbans) carried on for more than twenty years.

曹.note:
Cao Cao (155–220), from Qiao in Pei Kingdom. He raised troops at Chenliu in 189, became Administrator of Dong Commandery in 191, and in 192 became Governor of Yan Province and took in the Qing Province troops. In 196 he received Emperor Xian and made Xu the capital, holding the emperor hostage to command the lords.
He destroyed Lü Bu in 198, defeated Yuan Shao at Guandu in 200, took Ye in 204 and campaigned north against the Wuhuan in 207, unifying the north; in 208 he was checked at Red Cliffs. He became Duke of Wei in 213 and King of Wei in 216.
In 220 Cao Pi replaced the Han and founded Wei, with its capital at Luoyang. After Cao Rui's reign power gradually passed to the Sima family, and after the Incident at the Gaoping Tombs in 249 the Cao emperors were figureheads; Wei conquered Shu in 263 and abdicated in favour of Sima Yan in 265.

刘备.note:
Liu Bei (161–223), from Zhuo County in Zhuo Commandery, claimed descent from King Jing of Zhongshan. He rose fighting the Yellow Turbans and attached himself in turn to Gongsun Zan, Tao Qian, Lü Bu, Cao Cao, Yuan Shao and Liu Biao, holding Xu Province twice (194–196, 199–200).
In 208 he allied with Sun Quan against Cao Cao; after Red Cliffs he took the four commanderies of southern Jing and borrowed Nan Commandery, took Yi Province in 214 and Hanzhong in 219, proclaiming himself King of Hanzhong; in the same year Guan Yu lost Jing Province.
In 221 he proclaimed himself emperor at Chengdu with the dynastic name Han (known to history as Shu Han), and in 222 was crushed at Yiling. After his death in 223 Zhuge Liang ran the government, campaigned south and then launched five northern campaigns; Jiang Wei carried them on. In 263 the Wei army entered Shu and Liu Shan surrendered.

孙.note:
Sun Jian (155–191), Administrator of Changsha, rose against Dong Zhuo and was killed at Xiangyang. His son Sun Ce served Yuan Shu, crossed the Yangtze in 195 and within a few years held the six commanderies of Jiangdong; he was killed by assassins in 200 and his brother Sun Quan succeeded him.
Sun Quan allied with Liu Bei against Cao Cao at Red Cliffs in 208, seized Jing Province in 219 and defeated Liu Bei at Yiling in 222; he accepted the title King of Wu from Wei in 221, broke with Wei the next year, proclaimed himself emperor at Wuchang in 229 and soon moved his capital to Jianye.
In Sun Quan's last years a succession dispute weakened the state; his successors Sun Liang and Sun Xiu were both dominated by powerful ministers, and Sun Hao was a tyrant. In winter 279 Jin attacked Wu along six routes; Sun Hao surrendered the next year, and the Three Kingdoms passed to Jin.

晋.note:
In 249 Sima Yi staged the Incident at the Gaoping Tombs and killed Cao Shuang; Sima Shi and Sima Zhao then ran the Wei government in turn, crushed the Three Rebellions in Huainan and conquered Shu in 263. In the 12th month of 265 Sima Yan accepted the abdication of Wei, named his state Jin and kept Luoyang as his capital.
Jin put Yang Hu in charge of Jing Province and had Wang Jun build ships in Yi Province; in winter 279 it attacked Wu along six routes, and in the 3rd month of the next year Sun Hao surrendered, ending nearly a century of division that had begun with the Yellow Turbans.

西域都护.note: The Eastern Han opened the Western Regions three times. In 91 Ban Chao became Protector-General of the Western Regions, with his seat at Tuoqian City; after he subdued Karasahr in 94, the fifty-odd states of the Western Regions all sent hostages and submitted, the height of Han power there. The Protector-General was abolished in 107, and thereafter the region was managed off and on through the Chief Clerk of the Western Regions and the Wu-Ji Colonel.

行在.note: In the 7th month of 195 Emperor Xian left Chang'an for the east under the protection of Yang Feng, Dong Cheng and others; after a heavy defeat at Caoyang in the 12th month he crossed the Yellow River and stayed at Anyi in Hedong, not returning to Luoyang until the 7th month of the next year.

董卓.note: From Lintao in Longxi; he rose to power with the troops of Liang Province. Summoned by He Jin in 189, he entered the capital and quickly took control of the court, deposing the Young Emperor, setting up Emperor Xian and making himself Chancellor of State. In 190 the provinces and commanderies east of the passes rose against him; Dong Zhuo burned Luoyang and took the emperor west to Chang'an. He was killed by Wang Yun and Lü Bu in the 4th month of 192.

李傕.note: Former officers of Dong Zhuo. In 192, following Jia Xu's plan, they counterattacked Chang'an, killed Wang Yun, drove out Lü Bu and held Emperor Xian captive; later the two fell out, and Chang'an was left in ruins. Emperor Xian went east in 195; after 196 Li Jue fell back to Huangbai City, and in 198 he was killed by Duan Wei and others led by the Supervisor of Internuncios Pei Mao.

袁绍.note:
From Ruyang in Runan, of a family with "four generations of Three Excellencies". In 190 he was leader of the coalition east of the passes; in 191 he forced Han Fu to give up Ji Province, in 192 he defeated Gongsun Zan at Jieqiao, and in 199 he destroyed him, holding the four provinces of Ji, Qing, You and Bing with several hundred thousand armoured troops.
He was crushed at Guandu in 200 and died of illness in 202; his sons Yuan Tan and Yuan Shang fought each other and were destroyed in turn by Cao Cao (205–207).

袁谭.note: Yuan Shao's eldest son, Inspector of Qing Province. After Yuan Shao's death he fought his brother Yuan Shang for the succession, surrendered to Cao Cao for a time, rebelled again in 204, and was defeated and killed at Nanpi in the 1st month of 205.

韩馥.note: Governor of Ji Province and a member of the coalition east of the passes, he stayed at Ye to supply grain to the armies. In 191, squeezed between Yuan Shao and Gongsun Zan, he gave up Ji Province, and later killed himself in fear of what might befall him.

公孙瓒.note: From Lingzhi in Liaoxi; his White Horse Volunteers made him feared beyond the frontier. At odds with Liu Yu, Governor of You Province, he sent Tian Kai to contest Qing Province, and in 193 attacked and killed Liu Yu and took You Province. He was defeated by Yuan Shao at Jieqiao in 192 and again at Baoqiu in 195, fell back to hold Yijing, and burned himself to death when it fell in 199.

刘虞.note: A member of the Han imperial clan and Governor of You Province, he pacified the Wuhuan and Xianbei with lenient rule. He was killed by Gongsun Zan in 193; his son Liu He, with Xianyu Fu and Yan Rou, joined Yuan Shao and defeated Gongsun Zan in 195.

袁术.note: Yuan Shao's younger brother. He held Nanyang from 190, using Sun Jian as his vanguard against Dong Zhuo; defeated by Cao Cao in 193, he moved to Shouchun in Huainan. In 197 he proclaimed himself emperor with the dynastic name Zhong; he lived in boundless extravagance and debauchery, and his followers and kin deserted him; and in 199, trying to go north to Yuan Shao and blocked by Liu Bei, he coughed blood and died.

刘表.note: From Gaoping in Shanyang, one of the "Eight Talents". In 190 he rode alone into Jing Province, won over great families such as the Cai and the Kuai, and moved his seat to Xiangyang. He held Jing Province for nearly twenty years and kept it at peace, and many scholars from the north took refuge there. He died of illness in 208, and his younger son Liu Cong surrendered the province to Cao Cao; his elder son Liu Qi held Jiangxia and died of illness the next year.

刘焉.note: In 188 Liu Yan proposed "abolishing Inspectors and setting up Governors" and made himself Governor of Yi Province; once in Shu he cut the roads and quietly harboured ambitions of his own. He died in 194 and was succeeded by his son Liu Zhang, a weak ruler, who invited Liu Bei into Shu in 211 to resist Zhang Lu; in 214 Liu Bei besieged Chengdu and Liu Zhang surrendered.

张鲁.note: Third patriarch of the Way of the Five Pecks of Rice (the Way of the Celestial Masters). In 191 he seized Hanzhong on Liu Yan's orders, then made himself independent, governing the people through "libationers" in a unity of religion and government, and dominated Ba and Hanzhong for nearly thirty years. In 215 Cao Cao broke through Yangping Pass, and Zhang Lu sealed his storehouses and surrendered.

陶谦.note: Inspector and then Governor of Xu Province. Cao Cao attacked him twice, in 193 and 194, massacring the people around Pengcheng and Tan. He died of illness in winter 194, leaving Xu Province to Liu Bei.

吕布.note: From Jiuyuan in Wuyuan, a fierce warrior and fine horseman and archer. In 189 he killed Ding Yuan and joined Dong Zhuo, and in 192 he plotted with Wang Yun to kill Dong Zhuo. After Chang'an fell he fled east; in 194 he seized Yan Province while Cao Cao was campaigning in the east, after his own defeat went over to Liu Bei, and in 196 turned on him and took Xu Province by seizing Xiapi. In winter 198 Cao Cao besieged him at Xiapi; his officers seized Chen Gong and surrendered, and Lü Bu came down from the White Gate Tower to surrender and was strangled.

韩遂.note:
In 184 the Huangzhong Auxiliary Hu rose with Beigong Boyu, Bian Zhang and Han Sui, throwing Liang Province into turmoil; Ma Teng joined them in 187. In 192 Li Jue gave the two men general's titles; thereafter they nominally submitted to the Han while keeping their own armies in Liang Province and Guanzhong.
In 208 Ma Teng went to court and his son Ma Chao took over his troops; in 211 Ma Chao and Han Sui joined the Guanzhong generals against Cao Cao and were crushed at Tong Pass and Weinan. In 213 Ma Chao attacked Jicheng; the next year he was driven out by Yang Fu and Jiang Xu and went to Zhang Lu and then Liu Bei. Han Sui was killed by his own men in 215.

宋建.note: From Fuhan. When Liang Province rose in 184 he styled himself "King of the River's Source who Pacifies Han", proclaimed his own era, set up a full set of officials and held Fuhan for thirty years. In 214 Xiahou Yuan stormed and massacred Fuhan and Song Jian was killed.

公孙氏.note: Gongsun Du was made Administrator of Liaodong by Dong Zhuo in 189; the next year he set himself up as Marquis of Liaodong and Governor of Ping Province, attacking Goguryeo to the east and the Wuhuan to the west. His son Gongsun Kang beheaded Yuan Shang and Yuan Xi and sent their heads to Cao Cao (207), and split off the southern part of Lelang as Daifang Commandery. His grandson Gongsun Yuan beheaded the Wu envoys and submitted to Wei in 233, made himself King of Yan in 237, and was destroyed by Sima Yi in 238.

士燮.note:
From Guangxin in Cangwu; he became Administrator of Jiaozhi in 187. After Zhu Fu, Inspector of Jiao Province, was killed, Shi Xie had his brothers made Administrators: Shi Yi of Hepu, Shi Wei of Jiuzhen and Shi Wu of Nanhai, so that "the brothers all held commanderies and were masters of the province". The histories do not record Cangwu and Yulin as belonging to the Shi family, so the map does not count them.
Around the middle of the decade 200–209 the court sent Shi Xie a sealed letter making him General of the Household Who Pacifies the South, with oversight of the seven commanderies. In 210 Bu Zhi became Inspector of Jiao Province; Shi Xie and his brothers accepted his authority and sent a son as hostage.
Shi Xie died in 226 and Sun Quan split the region into Guang and Jiao provinces; Shi Xie's son Shi Hui made himself Administrator of Jiaozhi and defied the order; Lü Dai attacked and beheaded him. Shi Yi and Shi Wei were pardoned and made commoners, and a few years later were executed for some offence.

交州刺史.n: Inspectors of Jiao Province (Zhu Fu & Zhang Jin)
交州刺史.note:
Inspectors of Jiao Province sent by the court. Zhu Fu of Kuaiji appointed many men from his home region as officials, who oppressed the people; bandits rose everywhere, and he fled to the sea and died. His successor, Zhang Jin of Nanyang, joined Shi Xie in 203 in petitioning to turn the Jiaozhi Circuit into Jiao Province, was made Governor of Jiao Province, and governed from Guangxin in Cangwu. He made an enemy of Liu Biao, Governor of Jing Province, "weak in arms against a strong foe, raising troops year after year", and was later killed by his officer Ou Jing.
The map gives them only the two commanderies of Cangwu and Yulin: Shi Huang, Administrator of Cangwu, was not a Shi family appointee, and the histories do not say who held Yulin, so it goes with the Inspector for now. After Zhang Jin's death Liu Biao sent Lai Gong to replace him as Inspector and Wu Ju to replace Shi Huang as Administrator of Cangwu.

张杨.note: From Yunzhong; like Lü Bu, he served under Ding Yuan. He became Administrator of Henei in 192 and was based at Yewang; in 195 he helped Emperor Xian on his way east. In 198, wanting to rescue Lü Bu, he was killed by his officer Yang Chou; the remnants of his force, under Sui Gu, were destroyed by Cao Cao in 199.

刘岱.note: Inspector of Yan Province and a member of the coalition east of the passes, camped at Suanzao. In 190 he killed Qiao Mao, Administrator of Dong Commandery; in 192 he rashly gave battle to the Qing Province Yellow Turbans and was defeated and killed.

孔伷.note: Inspector of Yu Province and a member of the coalition east of the passes, camped in Yingchuan. He was known for his eloquence in pure conversation, and soon died of illness.

王匡.note: Administrator of Henei and a member of the coalition east of the passes, camped at Heyang Ford; Dong Zhuo's army routed him in 190.

张邈.note: Administrator of Chenliu, one of the "Eight Providers" and an old friend of Cao Cao. In 194 he and Chen Gong brought in Lü Bu to seize Yan Province; after their defeat he went to ask Yuan Shu for help and was killed by his own men. His brother Zhang Chao held Yongqiu, which fell in 195 and was massacred.

桥瑁.note: Administrator of Dong Commandery. In 190 he forged a letter from the Three Excellencies calling for action against Dong Zhuo, which set off the coalition east of the passes; he was killed by Liu Dai the same year.

鲍信.note: Chancellor of Jibei, the first in the coalition east of the passes to see Cao Cao's worth. In 192 he invited Cao Cao to take over Yan Province, and in the same year he died fighting hard against the Qing Province Yellow Turbans.

焦和.note: Inspector of Qing Province and a member of the coalition east of the passes; he soon died of illness, and Qing Province then became a battleground between Yuan Shao and Gongsun Zan.

孔融.note: A twentieth-generation descendant of Confucius and one of the Seven Masters of the Jian'an era. He was Chancellor of Beihai from 190 to 196; defeated by Yuan Tan in 196, he fled to Xu, and was killed by Cao Cao in 208.

刘繇.note: A member of the Han imperial clan, appointed Inspector of Yang Province in 194; since Yuan Shu held Shouchun, he crossed the Yangtze and governed from Qu'e. Defeated by Sun Ce in 195, he fell back to Yuzhang and died of illness in 197; Hua Xin, Administrator of Yuzhang, surrendered to Sun Ce in 199.

王朗.note: Administrator of Kuaiji; defeated by Sun Ce in 196, he fled to Dongye, later served Cao Wei and rose to Minister over the Masses.

张绣.note: From Wuwei, nephew of Zhang Ji. After Zhang Ji's death in 196 he took over his troops, camped at Wan and relied on Liu Biao. In 197 he surrendered to Cao Cao and then rebelled, killing Cao Ang and Dian Wei; in 199, on Jia Xu's advice, he surrendered to Cao Cao again.

黑山.note: The Black Mountain army, one of the Yellow Turban remnants, led by Zhang Yan of Changshan and said to number a million. Based in the Taihang Mountains, it raided Changshan, Zhao, Zhongshan, Shangdang, Henei and other commanderies; in 185 the Han gave Zhang Yan the title General of the Household Who Pacifies Disorder. In 205 Zhang Yan surrendered to Cao Cao with more than 100,000 followers.

扬州诸郡.note: Between 190 and 194 Yang Province had not yet fallen to any warlord: the Inspector Chen Wen (later Chen Yu) sat at Shouchun, while Lu Kang in Lujiang, Zhou Xin in Danyang, Xu Gong in Wu Commandery, Wang Lang in Kuaiji, Zhuge Xuan in Yuzhang and others each held their own commandery.

并州诸郡.note: Bing Province in the 190s: most of its northern commanderies were held by the Southern Xiongnu and the Xianbei, while around Taiyuan, Yanmen and Xihe Inspectors and Administrators appointed by the court barely kept control, with the Baibo and Black Mountain bands roaming between. After 199 it passed to Yuan Shao, who made his nephew Gao Gan Inspector.

河西诸郡.note: After the risings in Liang Province the Hexi Corridor was cut off from Guanzhong; Wuwei, Zhangye, Jiuquan, Dunhuang and the other commanderies were held by local strongmen or self-appointed Administrators, with no contact with the court for decades. In 220 Cao Pi sent Zhang Ji and Su Ze to put down the risings, and Hexi came under Wei.

北匈奴.note: Early in the Eastern Han the Xiongnu split into southern and northern branches. In 89 and 91 Dou Xian and Geng Kui twice routed the Northern Chanyu, at Mount Jiluo and in the Jinwei Mountains; the main body of the Northern Xiongnu moved west, and more than 100,000 tents that remained were absorbed by the Xianbei.

鲜卑.note:
Descendants of the Donghu. After the Northern Xiongnu went west, the Xianbei moved into the lands north of the Gobi, and the Xiongnu who remained "all called themselves Xianbei". In the mid-2nd century Tanshihuai united the tribes and set up his court at Mount Danhan; his realm stretched more than 12,000 li from east to west and was divided into eastern, central and western sections. The confederation broke up after his death in 181.
In the late Han and Three Kingdoms the bands of Budugen, Kebineng, Suli and others were active beyond the frontiers of You and Bing provinces; Kebineng was the strongest until 235, when Wang Xiong, the Wei Inspector of You Province, had him assassinated. Late in the Three Kingdoms period the Tuoba, Murong, Yuwen, Duan, Tufa and other tribes rose.

乌桓.note: Descendants of the Donghu; under the Eastern Han they moved into the frontier commanderies. In the late Han the strongest of the Wuhuan of Liaoxi, the Liaodong Dependent State and Youbeiping was Tadun of Liaoxi, who was allied with Yuan Shao by marriage. In 207 Cao Cao crushed them at White Wolf Mountain, beheaded Tadun and moved their people into the interior, and the Wuhuan, "the finest cavalry in the realm", were absorbed into Cao Cao's army.

南匈奴.note: The Southern Xiongnu submitted to the Han in 48 and settled at Meiji in Xihe. In 188 their people killed the Chanyu Qiangqu; his son Yufuluo stayed in the Central Plains, moving between Henei and Pingyang. In the late Han the northern frontier commanderies of Wuyuan, Yunzhong, Dingxiang and Shuofang were in fact held by the Xiongnu; in 216 Cao Cao kept the Chanyu Huchuquan at Ye and divided his people into five divisions settled across the commanderies of Bing Province.

羌.note: Qiang risings ran through almost the whole Eastern Han: three great risings, in 107, 140 and 159, cost the court tens of billions of cash. In the late Han the Qiang and Hu joined Han Sui and Ma Chao; in the Three Kingdoms Wei and Shu competed for them, and Jiang Wei repeatedly sought their support on his northern campaigns.

弃地.note: Endless Qiang risings in the middle and later Eastern Han forced Beidi, Shang Commandery and others to be moved inland again and again. In 215 Cao Cao also abolished the four commanderies of Yunzhong, Dingxiang, Wuyuan and Shuofang, keeping only one county from each, merged them into Xinxing Commandery and resettled it south of the Xing Ridge. From then on no commanderies or counties were set up in the Hetao and Ordos; Qiang, Hu and remnant Xiongnu lived there mixed together, and the histories call it abandoned land. Around 258 the Tuoba Xianbei moved to Shengle in the Yunzhong–Dingxiang area.

江淮弃地.note:
In 213 Cao Cao, fearing that Sun Quan would raid the commanderies along the Yangtze, ordered their people to move inland, causing panic: "from Lujiang, Jiujiang, Qichun and Guangling more than 100,000 households all crossed east of the river; the land west of the river was emptied, and south of Hefei only Wancheng remained" (Biography of the Lord of Wu).
From then on the land between Hefei and the Yangtze was a buffer zone between Wei and Wu. Both sides fought there repeatedly (Ruxu, Dongxing, Hefei New City), but neither held it for long. On the map Wei holds Hefei and Lu'an, Wu holds Wancheng and Ruxu Fort, and the rest is abandoned land.

夫余.note: An ancient kingdom in the Songhua River basin, on close terms with the Han. In the late Han it relied on the Gongsun clan of Liaodong, and Gongsun Du married a woman of his clan to its king.

高句丽.note: Founded on the middle reaches of the Hun and Yalu rivers, with its capital first at Heulseunggol Fortress and later at Hwando (Gungnae City). In the late Han it fought the Gongsun clan of Liaodong many times; in 244–245 Guanqiu Jian, the Wei Inspector of You Province, twice took Hwando and carved an inscription to record his victory.

西域诸国.note: In the later Eastern Han the posts of Chief Clerk of the Western Regions and Wu-Ji Colonel were set up and abolished by turns, and the states swallowed one another; the largest were Shanshan, Khotan, Kucha, Kashgar and Karasahr. From 222 Shanshan, Kucha, Khotan and others sent envoys to Wei; Wei and Jin stationed the Chief Clerk of the Western Regions at Loulan and the Wu-Ji Colonel at Gaochang.

林邑.note: In 192 Ou Lian of Xianglin County in Rinan Commandery killed the county magistrate, made himself king and founded Linyi (later known as Champa), which went on to raid Rinan and Jiuzhen many times.
